papers.title: Wearable sensor-based measures on light at day and night, rest-activity circadian rhythm and sleep, and mental health among Hong Kong nurses: a 7-day repeated-measures study.
Sleep.
Sleep and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Understanding the Bidirectional Relationship.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are pervasive across the spectrum of Lewy body disorders (LBDs), including Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Accumulating clinical, epidemiologic, and neurobiological evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between sleep dysfunction and neurodegeneration, in which pathologic processes disrupt sleep-wake regulation, and impaired sleep may exacerbate neurodegenerative mechanisms, including impaired proteostasis, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and failure of glymphatic clearance. In this review article, the authors synthesize evidence linking sleep and circadian disturbances with LBDs across prodromal, early, and advanced disease stages.

papers.title: Narcolepsy: Current State and Future Prospects.
papers.abstract: Narcolepsy is a chronic neurologic disorder that affects individuals throughout the entire 24-hour day, extending beyond its hallmark symptoms of excessive daytime sleepiness, disrupted night-time sleep, sleep-related hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and cataplexy in type 1 narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy often face significant academic, social, economic, and health-related challenges, along with difficulties accessing coordinated, individualized care. Although treatment options are expanding, guidance for tailoring therapy to symptom burden, life stage, and personal goals remains limited. Future care should adopt a transdisciplinary, patient-centered approach that addresses lifelong functional impacts and incorporates emerging therapies, including treatments targeting orexin-related pathophysiology.

papers.title: Persistent Hypersomnia in Neurological Disease: Mechanisms, Diagnosis, and Management.
papers.abstract: Hypersomnia in neurological disease is characterized by excessive sleep quantity in a day, distinct from excessive daytime sleepiness. It arises from the disruption of brainstem-hypothalamic-thalamic arousal circuits and neurotransmitter systems. Hypersomnia significantly impacts quality of life, safety, cognition, rehabilitation, and caregiver burden across conditions, including Parkinson's disease, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and multiple sclerosis. Systematic evaluation with polysomnography/multiple sleep latency testing distinguishes hypersomnia from fatigue and apathy. Treatment involves mechanism-guided approaches: addressing reversible causes (medications, sleep disorders), then pharmacotherapy with wake-promoting agents or stimulants, with special considerations for epilepsy, autonomic dysfunction, and neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythm Disruptions: Causes, Consequences, and Treatment Approaches.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are intrinsic biological cycles of approximately 24 h that regulate sleep, metabolism, hormone secretion, cardiovascular function, and other physiologic processes. Coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus and molecular clock genes such as CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY, these rhythms are influenced by external cues, especially light, meal timing, exercise, and social interactions. Circadian disruption contributes to sleep-wake disorders, metabolic dysfunction, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, psychiatric illness, and cancer risk. Assessment tools include melatonin measurements, questionnaires, sleep diaries, and actigraphy. Treatment focuses on optimizing zeitgebers, particularly light exposure and melatonin, to restore circadian alignment and improve health outcomes.

papers.title: Sleep Health and Well-being for the Neurologist.
papers.abstract: Burnout is highly prevalent in neurologists and may be linked to challenges with sleep health. Poor sleep quality, insufficient sleep, and undiagnosed sleep conditions may also contribute to reduced empathy, depression, and medical errors. Evidence from medical students, residents and practicing physicians shows that challenges with sleep often begin during training and may persist throughout a clinician's career. Cultural, occupational, and personal barriers frequently prevent the prioritization of sleep health. Improving sleep health through organizational support, healthy sleep habits, evaluation of sleep conditions, education and peer support can enhance clinician well-being, performance, resilience, and patient care.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Sleep.
papers.abstract: This article explores how generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models are impacting the practice of sleep medicine from data analysis to patient interaction. The various AI advances in the field should be recognized as tools that have the potential to enhance care through increasing diagnostic expertise and reducing administrative burden. However, application in clinical settings require clinician familiarity and oversight to mitigate risks. As AI usage has become so ubiquitous and accessible, clinicians must navigate the blurring lines between patient-generated and clinical data, while preparing for a future where usage of AI may become a medicolegal necessity.

papers.title: Sleep and Pain.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide and frequently co-occurs with insomnia. The relationship is bidirectional; chronic insomnia compromises endogenous pain modulatory processes, resulting in heightened pain sensitivity and diminished coping capacity, and chronic pain results in pain-related arousals and fragmented sleep, increasing the risk for insomnia. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is recommended as the first-line treatment of insomnia, and meta-analyses demonstrate efficacy for treating both insomnia and chronic pain compared to targeted pain protocols. This review discusses diagnostic considerations and treatment options, with particular attention to adaptations for vulnerable populations.

papers.title: Sleep and Aging: Understanding Changes and Promoting Healthy Sleep in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and disorders (e.g., sleep-disordered breathing and insomnia) are commonly observed in aging populations and are associated with numerous health conditions (e.g., cardiovascular disease) that can impede everyday functioning and well-being. Thus, this review focuses on conceptual frameworks accounting for various factors related to aging adults' sleep, benefits and challenges of using various sleep assessments across aging populations, and considerations for optimizing treatment efforts to improve their sleep health. With increased longevity and divergent life-course experiences, various diagnostic and treatment strategies will be necessary to develop personalized approaches to sustaining good sleep health.

papers.title: Innovative Treatments for Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: This article reviews current and emerging treatment options for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), emphasizing alternatives for patients who cannot tolerate continuous positive airway pressure. Established therapies include mandibular advancement devices, which mechanically enlarge the airway and weight-loss interventions that address a major modifiable risk factor. Newer approaches include daytime tongue stimulation, intraoral negative pressure therapy, nasal expiratory positive airway pressure devices, positional therapy, and orofacial myofunctional therapy. Implantable hypoglossal nerve stimulation systems, including Inspire and Food and Drug Administration-approved devices, offer effective treatment of patients with moderate-to-severe OSA. Together, these expanding options support a more personalized approach to OSA management.

papers.title: Pediatric Sleep Disorders: Early Identification and Management Strategies.
papers.abstract: This review highlights pediatric sleep disorders that can be identified early and treated effectively, emphasizing their impact on child health and quality of life. Key conditions discussed include obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), restless legs syndrome (RLS), sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE), and narcolepsy. This article discusses epidemiology, risk factors, clinical presentations, diagnostic approaches, complications and evidence-based treatments for each disorder. OSA is associated with neurocgnitive abd cardiovascular consequences, while RLS is strongly linked to low iron stores (ferritin). SHE requires prompt recognition to reduce seizure burden, and narcolepsy often presents atypically in children, causing diagnostic delays and significant psychosocial impact..

papers.title: Advancements in the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a common and clinically significant disorder characterized by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with associated daytime impairment. In patients with neurologic disease, insomnia contributes substantially to overall disease burden and demonstrates a bidirectional relationship, in which neurologic symptoms disrupt sleep and insomnia exacerbates neurologic symptom severity and functional outcomes. Although sleep disturbance may arise as a consequence of underlying disease, insomnia frequently emerges as a comorbid disorder that warrants independent recognition and treatment. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia remains the preferred first-line intervention, with the strongest evidence for sustained improvement.

papers.title: Restless Legs Syndrome: Current Concepts in Diagnosis and Treatment.
papers.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common sensorimotor disorder affecting approximately 7% of adults globally, with substantial impact on sleep and quality of life. This review covers the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and evidence-based management of RLS, with emphasis on recent developments: the 2025 American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) systematic review and guideline, and the consolidation of alpha-2-delta ligands as preferred first-line therapy. Alpha-2-delta ligands have replaced dopamine agonists as preferred first-line chronic therapy, given the significant long-term risk of augmentation. A stepwise approach that starts with identifying exacerbating factors, continues optimizing iron, then adds tailored pharmacotherapy, offers the best outcomes across the disease spectrum.

papers.title: Sleep-Wake Disturbances Following Traumatic Brain Injury: Clinical Importance and Practical Approaches to Screening and Management.
papers.abstract: This article underscores the high prevalence and clinical significance of posttraumatic brain injury (TBI) sleep disturbances while placing these disturbances within the broader neurobiological sequelae of brain injury. Although the evidence base is currently evolving, our findings support a mechanistically informed clinical workflow to guide assessment and management of post-TBI sleep disturbances-from early screening to targeted intervention and referral to specialized TBI-sleep expertise when warranted. This framework emphasizes a multidisciplinary model integrating neurology, sleep medicine, neurorehabilitation, and mental health professionals to address the complex interplay among sleep physiology, neural recovery, and psychiatric comorbidity.

papers.title: Updates in Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia characterized by dream enactment behaviors resulting from loss of normal REM sleep atonia. Increasingly, RBD is recognized not only as a sleep disorder but as a critical neurologic entity, strongly associated with α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative diseases This review highlights recent advances in the understanding of RBD across its clinical spectrum, diagnosis, pathophysiology, and emerging role as a biomarker of neurodegeneration. Current management focuses on safety and symptomatic control, while ongoing research explores disease-modifying therapies and positions RBD as a key platform for neuroprotective clinical trials.

papers.title: Sleep Disorders in Neurologic Conditions.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are common in the general population but are even more prevalent in patients with neurologic diseases. Maintaining good sleep quality is important for recovery, cognition and quality of life, but many patients with neurologic conditions face unique challenges in the quest to be the best sleeper they can be. This article will discuss common issues that need to be evaluated and treated in people with a history of stroke, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, headache, and neuromuscular disease.

papers.title: Clinical use of transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography in the motor system.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) has emerged as a powerful technique to investigate cortical physiology and network dynamics in vivo. By directly recording the cortical response to noninvasive brain stimulation, TMS-EEG enables the assessment of cortical inhibitory and excitatory mechanisms, oscillatory activity, and effective connectivity within large-scale network organization independently of the corticospinal output pathways. These properties make TMS-EEG particularly valuable for studying disorders affecting the motor system. This chapter reviews the principles of TMS-EEG in the motor system and summarizes its application in four major neurologic disorders leading to motor network dysfunction, including stroke, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Across these, TMS-EEG has provided novel insights into disease-specific mechanisms, including cortical disinhibition, network reorganization, diaschisis, pathologic oscillatory activity, and alterations in brain complexity. Furthermore, growing evidence suggests that TMS-EEG-derived measures are associated with clinically relevant outcomes such as motor impairment, recovery potential, disease progression, and treatment response. Although methodologic challenges and the need for larger and longitudinal cohorts remain, TMS-EEG represents a promising approach for characterizing network dysfunction and may contribute to future treatment strategies in neurology.

papers.title: Brain-computer interfaces in the motor system: The technologies.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) translate neural activity into control signals for external devices and neuromodulatory/actuator systems, offering new avenues to restore, rehabilitate, or augment motor function after neurologic injury and disease. The field's foundations lie in early demonstrations that volitional modulation of cortical neurons is possible (operant conditioning), resulting in direct brain-computer interfacing, which catalyzed decades of translational research. Clinical advances now span noninvasive scalp electroencephalography systems that pair sensorimotor rhythms or movement‑related cortical potentials with proprioceptive or functional electrical stimulation (FES) feedback for post‑stroke rehabilitation, to invasive electrocorticography and intracortical arrays enabling multi‑degree‑of‑freedom robotic control and, more recently, limb reanimation through intracortical‑to‑FES neuroprostheses. This chapter critically reviews (i) signal acquisition technologies (noninvasive and invasive), (ii) design considerations for motor BCIs (spatiotemporal resolution, latency, stability, artifacts, and clinical workflow), (iii) signal processing and artificial intelligence approaches for decoding intent, (iv) hybrid systems that integrate neural with peripheral signals such as EMG and inertial sensing, and (v) feedback modalities-from visual and auditory to proprioceptive and state‑dependent stimulation. We conclude with an outlook on minimally invasive implants, wearable sensors, and calibration‑lite artificial intelligence models, and discuss translational milestones and barriers toward routine clinical adoption in neurology and neurosurgery.

papers.title: Neurophysiologic techniques to investigate movement disorders: Polymyography, backaveraging, and event-related (de)synchronization.
papers.abstract: The current chapter explains recording techniques and analyses that can help in the differentiation and classification of movement disorders. It will touch on clinical indications, in case this helps to understand why certain approaches are advised, and explain the interpretation and possible pitfalls. Techniques include recordings of muscle activity and analysis of muscle activation patterns, and use more advanced techniques including combined corticomuscular recordings and analyses. Recordings from multiple muscles (polymyography, PMG) can help to evaluate activation patterns, to differentiate (functional) tremor and fast myoclonus and to evaluate axial jerks. Jerk-locked back-averaging is applied in myoclonus, jerky functional movement disorders, and tics. The direct coupling between movement (electromyography, EMG) and motor cortex activity (electroencephalography, EEG/magnetoencephalography, MEG) helps to distinguish these movement disorders. Event-related potentials (ERPs) or fields (ERFs) are averaged amplitude fluctuations of ongoing brain activity that are time-locked to specific events. In movement disorders, ERPs can reveal subtle changes in cortical activity that precede muscle activation. In cases in which power changes in response to the specific stimulus are not phase-locked, event-related desynchronization (ERD) or synchronization (ERS) capture such non-phase-locked changes in EEG or MEG signals.

papers.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation-electroencephalography - relation to motor physiology.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) in combination with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) opens up the possibility to measure brain responses to TMS. This is a relatively novel technology that significantly extends the longer-established technologies of TMS of the motor cortex (M1) and recording of motor evoked responses via electromyography. TMS-EEG of M1 results in a typical sequence of TMS-evoked responses (TEPs), such as the P30, N45, P60, N100, and P200. TEPs constitute spatiotemporally complex waveforms that arise from both local neuronal activation and recurrent neuronal activity propagated across multiple cortical and subcortical regions. Response components<70 ms are caused by direct TMS effects, while later responses are significantly contaminated by peripherally evoked potentials caused by the auditory and somatosensory inputs from the TMS pulse. P30 reflects local M1 excitability controlled by voltage-gated ion channels, while N45 and P60 reflect excitation-inhibition balance controlled by GABAAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Several recent studies demonstrate the emerging clinical utility of TMS-EEG responses in the diagnosis and outcome prediction of several motor disorders, such as motor stroke and Parkinson disease.

papers.title: Corticomuscular or electroencephalography-electromyography coherence and intermuscular or electromyography-electromyography coherence.
papers.abstract: The central nervous system and the peripheral effectors must work together to enable accurate and precise movement. Coherence analysis is a mathematical method used to assess the correlation between two recorded signals. In neurophysiology, corticomuscular coherence quantifies functional connectivity between the central nervous system and the peripheral effectors, while intermuscular coherence quantifies the degree of shared neural input to distinct motor units. This chapter begins with an overview of rhythmic activities related to motor control, such as the brain activities measured by electroencephalography or magnetoencephalography, and the muscle activities measured by electromyography. And then, we introduce the fundamental principles of coherence analysis and its computation. Finally, we discuss corticomuscular and intermuscular coherence, highlighting its characteristics and clinical significance, particularly in pathologic conditions. Despite its mathematical simplicity, coherence analysis provides valuable insights into the neurophysiologic mechanisms underlying motor control in healthy conditions and in neurologic disorders.

papers.title: Obesity in Aging.
papers.abstract: Obesity in older adults is a complex, multifactorial condition requiring a comprehensive approach. Standard body mass index thresholds are less reliable in this population due to the obesity paradox, where moderate overweight may be protective. The coexistence of obesity and sarcopenia worsens frailty and mortality, making lean mass preservation essential. Lifestyle interventions like quality nutrition, resistance exercise, sleep, and stress management remain the foundation of care. Weight loss medications offer significant weight loss but risk accelerating muscle loss if used without structured support. Social determinants, including food access, income, and isolation, must be addressed for treatment to be truly effective.

papers.title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for sleep disorders in psychiatry.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are prevalent among psychiatric patients and are strongly associated with neurobiological, psychological, and behavioral processes. This chapter analyzes neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE), an approach incorporating the insights gained from neuroscience with patient education to understand and manage sleep disturbances better. To establish a scientific basis for psychoeducational interventions, we discuss central mechanisms of sleep regulation such as circadian rhythms, sleep homeostasis, neurotransmitter systems, and brain networks. It illustrates how bidirectional sleep disorders and psychiatric syndromes, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are linked, and explains sleep disturbance as a transdiagnostic key clinical feature. In addition to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, NIPE is used to provide a solution to insomnia by integrating mindfulness-based strategies and personalized interventions with the assistance of digital technologies. Implementation challenges and outcome assessment, as well as ethical dimensions of practice, are also considered. In fact, NIPE is a clinically relevant strategy that can both maximize patient engagement and ameliorate sleep disorder outcomes.

papers.title: [Pathological mechanism of cardiovascular disease complicated with insomnia mediated by heart Yin deficiency and TCM intervention strategies].
papers.abstract: The bidirectional comorbidity of insomnia and cardiovascular diseases(CVD) has become an urgent challenge in the prevention and control of chronic diseases in the global public health field, and the two conditions form a vicious cycle of reciprocal causation and mutual exacerbation. Conventional modern medicine mostly adopts a divide-and-conquer diagnostic and therapeutic strategy for this comorbidity. However, it is restricted by single-target mechanisms and accompanied by potential therapeutic conflicts of cross-system combined medication, which makes it difficult to fundamentally block the core pathological interaction cascade of comorbidity, and there is still room for improvement in overall clinical outcomes. The core theories of TCM, namely "the heart governs blood and vessels" and "the heart governs the mind", integrate the regulation of blood and vessel harmony and sleep-wake tranquility under the functional domain of the heart. This holistic cognitive system of "unity of vessels and spirit" provides a unique theoretical perspective for breaking through the limitations of modern comorbidity diagnosis and treatment. Combined with the regional pathological characteristics of Qi consumption and Yin damage due to high temperature and humidity as well as the morbidity patterns of the local population in the Lingnan region, this study identified heart Yin deficiency as the core pathological hub mediating the bidirectional comorbidity of CVD and insomnia. The progressive impairment of the three core physiological functions of heart Yin, namely nourishing, tranquilizing, and descending-purging, serves as the core driving link throughout the entire course of the comorbidity. The study established a three-stage dynamic pathogenesis evolution model, namely "the initiation stage of Yin deficiency and nourishment impairment→the progression stage of deficiency-fire disturbing the mind→the end stage of stasis-toxin intermingling". It systematically revealed the intrinsic consistency between the connotations of TCM pathogenesis at each stage and modern pathological mechanisms, including autonomic nervous system dysfunction, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal(HPA) axis dysfunction, inflammatory immune activation, and oxidative stress imbalance. Based on the above theories, the study proposed stepped precise TCM intervention strategies with nourishing heart Yin as the core therapeutic principle applied throughout the entire disease course. It integrated oral TCM and characteristic non-pharmacological therapies such as acupuncture and ear acupoint pressing, incorporated Lingnan-specific diagnostic and therapeutic experience, and constructed a comprehensive intervention system with multi-target and multi-pathway synergistic regulation. This strategy further enriches the academic connotations of "combination of disease and syndrome" and "holistic regulation" in TCM, and provides novel theoretical references and generalizable practical approaches for the integrated Chinese and western medicine clinical management of CVD complicated with insomnia.

papers.title: Relative Contribution of Individual and Environmental Determinants of Sleep in a French Adult Population.
papers.abstract: Insufficient sleep is a major public health concern. Many factors influence sleep, including light exposure, physical activity, and the bedroom environment. The objective of this observational study was to identify the main factors influencing sleep. A total of 195 healthy participants (61% female; 22-74 years) were monitored for eight consecutive days. Environmental, physiological and behavioural variables (light exposure, heart rate, physical activity, and bedroom conditions) and individual characteristics (age, sex, chronotype, and anxiety level) were collected. Regression tree models were used to identify the main determinants of sleep quality. Sleep efficiency was mainly influenced by sex, with women showing a higher efficiency (88% vs. 85%). In men, anxiety was associated with lower sleep efficiency (77% vs. 85%), whereas in women, nighttime noise ≥ 40 dB was associated with reduced sleep efficiency (85% vs. 89%). Slow wave sleep was determined by age and sleep timing, reaching 16% in individuals aged ≥ 50 years, 19% in those aged 34-50 years, and 23% in younger individuals with an earlier sleep midpoint. A later sleep midpoint (≥ 4.3 h) was associated with more nocturnal awakenings (57 vs. 38). Total sleep time was higher in women than men (414 vs. 382 min). This study suggests that both environmental and individual factors are associated with sleep quality and emerged as key determinants of sleep outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of considering both types of factors in sleep and support more personalized approaches to intervention. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and better characterize sleep determinants.

papers.title: Cognitive capacity in subjective cognitive decline: Insights from electrophysiological markers and dual-task performance.
papers.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) refers to self-reported cognitive deficits in the absence of objective cognitive impairment. Evidence suggests that neural changes may precede performance declines, highlighting the potential of electroencephalography (EEG) to detect early cognitive declines. Electrophysiological markers and changes in cognitive and motor performance were examined during dual-task performance to better understand the neural mechanisms underlying SCD. Older adults with (n=20) and without (n=20) SCD performed a working memory and finger tapping task simultaneously (i.e., dual task) and alone (i.e., single cognitive or motor). Linear mixed models were used to assess task and group effects for behavioural performance and EEG measures, including mean amplitude and power spectral density, in frontal, central, and parietal regions of interest (ROI). P2 and P3b mean amplitude were smaller during the dual task compared to single cognitive task. Additionally, the SCD group exhibited higher theta power overall and higher alpha power in each task and ROI compared to the non-SCD group. Higher power was observed during the dual task compared to single tasks except in the alpha band where the opposite was observed. Cognitive and motor performance decreased between single and dual tasks, and slower finger tapping speed was observed in the SCD compared to the non-SCD group. Neural and performance findings support the capacity sharing model of attention and may reflect the use of compensatory mechanisms in the SCD group. Electrophysiological changes may precede objective cognitive deficits and have the potential to complement existing approaches to characterizing SCD but must be examined longitudinally.

papers.title: Glymphatic dysfunction in epilepsy: imaging assessment, comorbidities, pathophysiology, and emerging therapeutic perspectives.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder driven by complex, multifactorial mechanisms, yet seizures remain uncontrolled in a substantial proportion of patients despite treatment. The glymphatic system, a brain-wide cerebrospinal fluid-interstitial fluid exchange pathway that facilitates metabolic waste clearance, has emerged as an important regulator of cerebral homeostasis. Accumulating experimental and neuroimaging evidence suggests that glymphatic-related processes may be involved in epileptogenesis and disease progression, although their precise roles remain to be established. This narrative review summarizes advances in the assessment of glymphatic-related processes and synthesizes findings across epilepsy subtypes. We examine how these findings relate to cognitive, sleep, and psychiatric comorbidities, as well as treatment outcomes. We interpret findings from complementary imaging approaches in their clinical context, considering epilepsy phenotype and disease course alongside accompanying white matter and network changes. This synthesis highlights the potential clinical significance of these findings and the limitations of current evidence while distinguishing observed associations from proposed mechanisms. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies as hypotheses for testing and outline considerations for initial proof-of-concept studies. Because most clinical studies rely on indirect imaging markers and include small patient cohorts, causal relationships and the clinical utility of these markers remain uncertain. Future studies combining standardized multimodal imaging, experimental models, and prospective clinical cohorts are needed to clarify underlying mechanisms and establish the clinical value of glymphatic-related findings in epilepsy.

papers.title: Cerebellar structural and electrophysiological alterations associated with neuropathic pain in mice.
papers.abstract: The cerebellum is increasingly implicated in pain, yet direct electrophysiology in neuropathy is scarce. We tested whether sciatic nerve chronic constriction injury (CCI) alters cerebellar dynamics and structure. Adult male mice underwent CCI, von Frey testing, structural MRI, spontaneous LFP recordings in lobules IV-V, and spontaneous/evoked single-unit recordings under anesthesia. CCI produced rapid, persistent mechanical hypersensitivity. Deformation-based morphometry (DBM) revealed regional volumetric alterations including localized contractions in the IV-V cerebellar lobules. Spontaneous LFPs showed reduced absolute δ/θ power, with unchanged relative (normalized) power, while β/γ were unchanged. Multi-unit activity in CCI mice exhibited higher firing rates, shorter inter-spike intervals, and larger spike amplitudes. Peripheral stimulation evoked larger responses in CCI. Neuropathic pain is associated with structural remodeling, suppressed spontaneous slow-band cerebellar activity and enhanced unit/evoked responsiveness, which we interpret, as a working hypothesis, as a low-synchrony/high-gain operating regime. These structural and electrophysiological changes are candidate signatures that motivate future mechanistic and causal studies of cerebellar involvement in neuropathic pain.

papers.title: Associations of academic time burden with depressive and anxiety symptoms in adolescents: A prospective multi-analytical study based on the Guangzhou Children and Adolescents Cohort.
papers.abstract: Academic pressure is a pervasive source of stress among secondary school students, and has been linked to higher risks of depression and anxiety. However, the association of academic time burden with depressive and anxiety symptoms, and the behavioral and symptom-level patterns involved, remain insufficiently understood. Using data from the Guangzhou Children and Adolescents Cohort, this study aimed to investigate whether self-reported academic time was longitudinally associated with elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms among adolescents. We curated the homework time, tutoring time, health-related behaviors, and depressive (CES-D-20) and anxiety (GAD-7) symptoms reported by participants, yielding depression (n = 9671, 44.7% girls) and anxiety (n = 4680, 41.1% girls) cohorts. Mixed-effects regression showed that longer homework time was significantly associated with both elevated depressive (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.03-1.15 per hour increase) and anxiety symptoms (OR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.02-1.19), with similar patterns for tutoring time (depressive: OR = 1.04, 95% CI: 1.01-1.08; anxiety: OR = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.10-1.21). Sleep duration mediated 20.4% and 26.9% of the associations of homework time with depressive and anxiety symptoms, respectively. The corresponding proportions for tutoring time were 9.5% and 2.1%, with the latter being non-significant. Network analysis revealed that baseline academic time was associated with somatic symptoms and uncontrollable worry during follow-up, and that anxiety and depressive symptoms were reciprocally associated over time. These findings add to the rationale for policies that regulate academic time and highlight sleep protection as a promising target for adolescent mental health.

papers.title: Circadian Gating of Neuroimmune Memory: A Shared Persistence-and-Gating Hypothesis for Chronic Pain, Depression, and Postoperative Cognitive Dysfunction.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain, depression, and postoperative cognitive dysfunction provide distinct settings in which inflammatory responses and persistent vulnerability may intersect. Evidence for specific cytokine, synaptic, and microglial mechanisms differs across these conditions and does not establish a single comorbidity mechanism. We examine whether circadian context influences the formation or later expression of neuroimmune memory. Circadian regulation of inflammatory responses and innate immune memory each have experimental support, while their coupling in disease-relevant microglia remains unresolved. Human BCG vaccination studies provide a peripheral timing-and-training precedent, which cannot be assumed to operate in the brain. We distinguish immune memory from ongoing inflammation, neuronal chromatin regulation, and sustained symptoms, and separate cell-autonomous microglial timing from rhythmic environmental inputs. The framework generates distinct tests of imprint formation, maintenance, recall, and reversal. A convincing test requires a resolved first challenge, control of initial inflammatory exposure and recall phase, and cell-resolved molecular measurements coupled to altered secondary-response function. Failure to reverse an established imprint would not exclude a role for timing during its formation. Perioperative studies offer a defined exposure but must distinguish delirium from longer-term cognitive decline. This evidence-calibrated hypothesis specifies what must be demonstrated before circadian interventions can be linked to prevention or modification of neuroimmune memory.

papers.title: A Metabolite-Centered Framework for Microbiota-Gut-Brain Communication Linking Constrained Signaling to Behavior and Stress Physiology.
papers.abstract: The microbiota-gut-brain axis links gut microbial activity with host neurophysiology and behavior, but its mechanistic interpretation remains fragmented across individual metabolites, biological compartments, and experimental systems. Here, we propose a metabolite-centered conceptual framework that organizes current evidence according to the constraints that determine whether microbial metabolic activity is translated into host effects, including metabolite production and host transformation, bioavailability and barrier access, host sensing, cross-system integration, and ultimately phenotype. Using short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolic pathways, bile acids, neurotransmitter-related compounds, and emerging microbial signals as representative examples, we synthesize evidence for receptor-mediated, metabolic, neuroimmune, neuroendocrine, and barrier-dependent mechanisms. We further distinguish microbiota-level from metabolite-specific causality and preclinical from human evidence across stress reactivity, affective and stress-coping responses, social interaction, learning and memory, feeding, and sleep/circadian regulation. Finally, we evaluate the translational potential of metabolite-targeted interventions and biomarkers while highlighting unresolved challenges related to source attribution, bioavailability, species translation, and causal inference. Rather than providing another catalogue of microbial metabolites, this Review presents a mechanistic framework that links microbial metabolism to neural and behavioral outcomes while identifying the evidence needed to advance toward reproducible and clinically relevant applications.

papers.title: Commercially available multimodal LLMs for EEG-based prognostication after cardiac arrest.
papers.abstract: Machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have been successfully applied to EEG-based prognostication in comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA), but typically rely on task-specific signal processing, feature extraction, and model development. Here, we investigated whether two commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs) could predict neurological outcome directly from EEG images. Thirty-three comatose patients on the first day after CA from a prospective cohort were included. For each patient, a single 10-second EEG segment displayed using a longitudinal bipolar montage was rendered as PNG image. ChatGPT 5.4. and Claude Opus 4.7 were instructed to estimate the probability for favorable outcome for each case based on the EEG and a generic information block describing conditions of recordings. Five different prompting strategies were used, including few-shot prompting where four exemplary EEGs (not from the 33 patients) were provided. Predictive performance was quantified using AUC and accuracy. Across prompting strategies, the AUC ranged from 0.86 to 0.99 for ChatGPT and from 0.74 to 1.00 for Claude. The highest accuracy achieved by both models was 93.9% using few-shot prompting. As reference, a previously published dedicated deep-learning model achieved 100% on the same cohort. In this exploratory study of a small cohort, multimodal LLMs showed variable but potentially promising discrimination for predicting favorable outcome from single EEG image in comatose patients after CA. Performance depended substantially on prompt design. These findings require confirmation in a larger cohort.

papers.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials investigating cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia in stroke and traumatic brain injury populations.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is highly prevalent following stroke and traumatic brain injury (TBI), and can contribute to challenges with mood, psychological functioning and quality of life. Emerging evidence supports the efficacy of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) for those who have experienced stroke or TBI, however a broader review incorporating sleep and mood-related outcomes has not yet been conducted. A systematic literature search was performed on Scopus, PubMed, Embase, and PsycINFO databases. Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2.0 tool. Random-effects meta-analyses calculating pooled effect sizes were performed, alongside assessment of heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses. Nine randomised controlled trials were included, with seven contributing to the primary meta-analysis. CBT-I was associated with lower insomnia disorder severity on the ISI (MD = -3.07, 95% CI [-4.46; -1.67], p = 0.0037) and lower sleep disturbance on the PSQI (MD = -1.81, 95% CI [-2.82; -0.80], p = 0.0058). Secondary analyses demonstrated a small, significant effect on anxiety symptoms (Hedges' g = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.49; -0.12], p = 0.0106), and a small-moderate non-significant effect on depressive symptoms (Hedges' g = -0.36, 95% CI [-0.84; 0.12], p = 0.1146). CBT-I appears a promising intervention for improving insomnia after stroke or TBI, with additional modest benefits for depression and anxiety.

papers.title: Brain border-associated macrophages rhythmically scavenge amyloid-beta and regulate vascular amyloid pathology.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruptions perturb the brain and immune system and increase the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet whether this involves dysregulation of brain immunity remains less clear. Here, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of the brain immune compartment around the day-night cycle and identified brain border-associated macrophages (BAMs) as highly rhythmic cells. We found that the rest phase was a specialized time for BAM engulfment, characterized by upregulation of endocytic machinery and enhanced uptake of fluid-borne material including amyloid-beta (Aβ). Rhythmicity in BAM scavenging was regulated by the clock gene Bmal1, mediated by the scavenger receptor CD206, and perturbed with age. In a mouse model of AD, deletion of Bmal1 in BAMs worsened perivascular and leptomeningeal Aβ plaque burden. Our results characterize rapid endocytosis as a specialized and rhythmic BAM function and identify perturbed timing of brain border immunity as one avenue by which circadian disruptions may precipitate amyloidosis.

papers.title: Effects of pharmacotherapy on quantitative electroencephalogram measures of sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: Recent studies of noradrenergic and antimuscarinic agents to treat obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) have been promising, but their impact on subjective and objective sleep quality and daytime sleepiness have shown inconsistent results. This study aimed to assess the effects of the noradrenergic agent reboxetine alone and in combination with the antimuscarinic oxybutynin on next-day objective sleepiness through quantitative analysis of wake electroencephalography (qEEG) during a Karolinska Drowsiness Test (KDT). This was a secondary analysis from a randomised trial of reboxetine alone and in combination with oxybutynin versus placebo in 16 participants with OSA. All participates have undergone a KDT in the evening prior to drug or placebo administration and sleep opportunity, and ∼1hr post-waking next morning. Mixed models were used to examine drug effects on qEEG outcomes. There was no significant main effect of treatment (Reboxetine vs placebo vs Reboxetine-Oxybutynin) on slow EEG frequencies or theta/alpha ratio during the morning KDT. There was a significant main effect of testing time (evening vs morning) with higher morning delta and theta EEG power during eyes open and the delta power during entire KDT (all p < 0.001) compared to the evening test. There was a significant main effect of electrode position (F3, C3, O1), on wake delta and theta EEG with both frequencies higher in frontal (F3) vs occipital regions (O1) (all p < 0.001). There were no interaction effects and no correlations between qEEG outcomes and morning subjective sleepiness. Reboxetine with and without oxybutynin did not increase neurophysiological markers of next-day morning sleepiness as measured by wake delta and theta EEG power. These findings support the potential safety profile of these agents in respect to next-day sleepiness in people with OSA.

papers.title: A mathematical programming approach for the robust resolution of superpositions of action potentials.
papers.abstract: Resolving the superposition of action potentials in neural recordings is essential for precise spike sorting, a key step in decoding neural activity. This study presents a novel mathematical programming approach to address this challenge. Our objective is to improve the accuracy and efficiency of superposition resolution by reformulating the problem as a quadratic mixed-integer programming problem. We developed a new framework that flexibly incorporates physiological constraints and adapts to various types of recordings. We validated our method using both simulated and experimental intramuscular electromyographic and neural signals. The performance was evaluated against the branch-and-bound algorithm, a leading method for resolving superpositions, focusing on accuracy and computational speed. We also tested its ability to handle complex cases, such as multiple occurrences of the same action potential, and leveraged multi-channel recordings to maintain high accuracy when some of the action potentials were unknown to the solver. Our approach successfully resolved superpositions of up to 15 action potentials with an accuracy exceeding 97%. It uniquely handles complex cases where the same action potential discharges multiple times, achieving 95% accuracy even with up to six repeated discharges of five distinct action potentials. Using 32-channel recordings, we maintained an identification rate of 94.6% for superpositions of five action potentials, even when 80% of the action potentials in the superpositions were unknown, demonstrating the framework's robustness to unknown action potentials interference. The proposed mathematical programming approach significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of superposition resolution, especially in complex and challenging scenarios. This methodology offers a robust and flexible tool that can advance neural signal processing and our understanding of neural dynamics.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine

papers.title: DMM-Net: A dual-stage multimodal modulation network for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) typically progresses from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and eventually to AD. Due to the overlap of imaging manifestations and clinical indicators across different stages, accurate multi-class diagnosis remains challenging. Although structured clinical data can provide complementary information to imaging modalities, effective collaborative modeling between three-dimensional structural magnetic resonance imaging (3D sMRI) and structured clinical data remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to develop a cross-modal modulation approach for AD diagnosis. In this study, a Dual-stage Multimodal Modulation Network (DMM-Net) was proposed for AD cognitive state classification by integrating 3D sMRI and structured clinical data. The proposed framework consists of a Position-aware Clinical Spatial Modulation (PCSM) module, a transfer learning-based three-dimensional imaging feature extraction network MedNet, and a Feature-Clinical Cross-modal Modulation (FCCM) module. At the shallow stage, PCSM combines an image-derived spatial response with a subject-level clinical bias to modulate early imaging features. At deeper stages, FCCM jointly uses the intermediate Layer2 imaging representation and the clinical embedding to generate stage-specific calibration parameters for Layer3 and Layer4. Experimental results on the ADNI dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of DMM-Net for the CN/MCI/AD three-class classification task. The combined PCSM-FCCM configuration achieved a BA of 75.1%, outperforming either module alone. Compared with the adapted HyperFusion baseline under the unified evaluation protocol, DMM-Net improved BA and precision by 9.0 and 7.7 percentage points, respectively. Post hoc Grad-CAM and SHAP analyses were used to characterize the imaging regions and structured clinical features associated with the model predictions. The framework enhances joint modeling between 3D sMRI and structured clinical data through a coordinated dual-stage multimodal modulation mechanism, demonstrating its effectiveness for multimodal computer-aided classification of Alzheimer's disease under the evaluated setting.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine

papers.title: A changing educational gradient in age-related sleep duration trajectories across birth cohorts.
papers.abstract: Sleep duration is shaped by both aging and historical context, yet little is known about how age-related sleep trajectories vary across birth cohorts and how these patterns differ by educational attainment and sex. Drawing on a life-course perspective, I examine age and cohort variation in sleep duration and assesses how the educational gradient in sleep duration - that is, differences in sleep duration across educational groups - has changed across generations. Data come from six waves of the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS, 2010-2022). The analytic sample includes 44,379 adults contributing 134,142 person-wave observations. Hierarchical linear models were used to estimate age and cohort trajectories in sleep duration and to examine educational and sex differences in these patterns. Sleep duration declined with age across adulthood and was lower among later-born cohorts than among earlier-born cohorts at comparable ages. Educational attainment further differentiated these age and cohort patterns. Among earlier-born cohorts, adults with higher levels of education reported shorter sleep duration than their less educated peers. This gradient progressively narrowed across successive cohorts, with the relative ordering of educational groups changing at younger cohort-age combinations. Although the cohort pattern was broadly similar among women and men, formal interaction tests indicated sex differences in the age- and cohort-related educational gradients. Additional analyses showed that the changing educational gradient was not materially altered after accounting for observed family, employment, economic, work-time, and health characteristics. Overall, these findings show that educational inequalities in sleep duration are historically contingent, highlighting the importance of linking life-course processes to social change in understanding how the meaning of socioeconomic position and health inequalities evolves across generations.

papers.title: Sleep nudges: A scoping review of choice architecture interventions to address sleep health.
papers.abstract: Sleep-related problems affect 40-60% of adults globally, contributing to significant health and economic burdens. Choice architecture interventions, which structure decision environments to promote beneficial behaviors without restricting choice, have been studied in various health domains but remain relatively unexplored in the field of sleep. This scoping review mapped existing evidence on choice architecture interventions aimed at modifying sleep-related behaviors to improve sleep health outcomes, categorized interventions according to established taxonomies, and identified research gaps. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we systematically searched three databases, identifying six articles containing eight individual studies that met the inclusion criteria, reflecting the limited evidence available. Studies varied in design (predominantly randomized controlled trials), populations (children to adults), and intervention approaches. Most interventions combined multiple strategies, pairing information provision with micro-incentives (monetary or academic) or commitment facilitation. Primary outcomes focused on sleep duration, quality, and hygiene, assessed via actigraphy-based monitoring or self-report. Key gaps include limited population and technique diversity, multicomponent designs preventing component isolation, the assessment of individual sleep outcomes rather than sleep health from a multidimensional perspective, limited evaluation of the effects of these interventions on overall health, and minimal long-term follow-up.

papers.title: The effect of web-based education and therapeutic play methods provided to children undergoing elective surgery on preoperative anxiety and fear, and postoperative pain and sleep: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of combining web-based education provided at home with therapeutic play implemented in the hospital on preoperative anxiety and fear, as well as postoperative pain and sleep, in children aged 7-12 years undergoing elective surgery. Randomized controlled experimental study. The study included 78 children aged 7-12 years who underwent elective surgery. The children were randomly assigned to two groups: intervention (n = 37) and control (n = 41). Children in the intervention group received web-based education about the surgical process at home and information through therapeutic play at the hospital, whereas the control group received standard preoperative nursing care. Data were collected using the Modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale-Short Form (mYPAS-SF), Child Fear Scale (CFS), Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale (WBFPS), and Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC). The preoperative mYPAS-SF and CFS scores, as well as the postoperative WBFPS scores, were significantly lower in the intervention group than in the control group (p < 0.05), with effect sizes indicating large clinical significance. No significant difference was found between the groups in terms of post-discharge SDSC scores (p > 0.05), and the effect size was clinically small. Providing preoperative preparation education using a combination of web-based education and therapeutic play was effective in reducing preoperative anxiety and fear and postoperative pain in children undergoing elective surgery; however, it did not affect improving sleep. Pediatric nurses can help reduce children's preoperative anxiety, fear, and postoperative pain in children scheduled for surgery by using effective, practical, web-based educational and therapeutic play methods tailored to the children's age and developmental characteristics in pediatric surgery clinics.

papers.title: A 6-week vegan Mediterranean diet reduces neutrophil count and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio compared with a traditional Mediterranean diet in women with fibromyalgia: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia (FM) is associated with a low-grade pro-inflammatory profile, reflected by elevated neutrophil counts and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), that may impair function. Evidence on the effects of a vegan Mediterranean diet on inflammation, functional outcomes, and quality of life remains limited. This secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of a 6-week vegan Mediterranean diet vs a traditional Mediterranean diet in women with FM on inflammatory and functional outcomes, with particular focus on NLR and functional performance. We hypothesized that a vegan Mediterranean diet would reduce neutrophil count and NLR more than a traditional Mediterranean diet in women with FM. Twenty-five women with FM were initially randomly assigned to either the traditional Mediterranean group (n = 12) or the vegan Mediterranean group (n = 13). Both diets were isocaloric and matched for macronutrient distribution. The outcomes evaluated included the NLR, white blood cell count, functional performance (Five-Times-Sit-To-Stand [FTSTS] and Timed Up and Go [TUG], kinesiophobia [Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia], sleep quality [Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index] and fatigue [Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory]). Compared to the traditional Mediterranean diet, the vegan Mediterranean diet significantly reduced NLR (P = .026; ES = 0.23) and neutrophil count (P = .037; ES = 0.21). However, no significant between-group differences were observed for kinesiophobia, sleep quality, fatigue or functional performance. A vegan Mediterranean diet improves systemic inflammatory profile, reflected by reductions in NLR and neutrophil count, in women with FM compared with a traditional Mediterranean diet. Longer-term studies are needed to confirm whether these changes translate into functional improvements.

papers.title: Machine-learning-assisted screening prioritization for MoCA-BC-defined mild cognitive impairment among rural older adults in China: a multicentre cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To develop and internally-externally validate a machine-learning-assisted model for identifying MoCA-BC-defined MCI screening-positive status among rural older adults in China and examine its potential use for nursing screening prioritization. We analyzed a multicentre cross-sectional survey of 551 community-dwelling rural adults aged 60 years or older from three regions in China. Screening-positive status was defined using education-stratified Montreal Cognitive Assessment-Basic (MoCA-BC) cut-offs, while MoCA-BC scores and cognitive-domain items were not used as predictors. Logistic regression, elastic net, random forest and XGBoost were compared using leave-one-region-out validation. Discrimination, Brier score, calibration, decision-curve analysis and grouped SHAP interpretation were evaluated. Overall, 143 participants (25.95%) were classified as MoCA-BC-defined MCI screening-positive. XGBoost showed the highest mean held-out-region AUC (0.943), whereas random forest had the lowest mean Brier score (0.099); the corresponding XGBoost mean Brier score was 0.102. XGBoost had a pooled calibration intercept of -0.213 and slope of 0.585, indicating imperfect calibration. Data-derived thresholds of 0.20 and 0.40 were explored as screening-priority operating points rather than prognostic risk cut-offs. The most influential feature groups were IADL function, education, BMI, sleep quality, age and depressive symptoms. Routinely collectable multidomain information may help nurses and primary-care workers prioritize rural older adults for standardized cognitive assessment. The model should be considered a preliminary pre-screening aid rather than a substitute for MoCA-BC or comprehensive clinical diagnosis. Independent prospective validation, local recalibration and implementation testing are required before routine use.

papers.title: Sleep disturbance and functional disability mediate the association between chronic lower back pain and presenteeism in long-haul bus drivers.
papers.abstract: Objectives. Chronic lower back pain (CLBP) is highly prevalent among long-haul bus drivers and is associated with reduced work productivity. This study examined whether sleep disturbance and functional disability sequentially mediate the relationship between CLBP and presenteeism. Methods. The cross-sectional study included 167 professional long-haul bus drivers (CLBP, n = 67; non-CLBP, n = 100). Pain intensity, functional disability, sleep disturbance and presenteeism were assessed using the visual analog scale, Oswestry disability index, Jenkins sleep scale and Stanford presenteeism scale, respectively. Serial multiple mediation analysis (Hayes PROCESS Model 6) with 5000 bootstrap resamples was performed. Results. Drivers with CLBP had significantly higher pain intensity, functional disability, sleep disturbance and presenteeism than those without CLBP (all p < 0.001). CLBP was significantly associated with presenteeism (B = 2.51, p < 0.001). However, after including sleep disturbance and functional disability as sequential mediators, the direct effect became non-significant (B = 0.30, p = 0.718), indicating full mediation. Functional disability was the primary mediator, while the serial pathway through sleep disturbance and functional disability was also significant. Conclusion. CLBP affects work productivity primarily through functional disability, whereas sleep disturbance indirectly contributes by worsening disability. Interventions targeting both functional restoration and sleep may reduce presenteeism in long-haul bus drivers.
papers.journal: International journal of occupational safety and ergonomics : JOSE

papers.title: Validation of the BASED Score as a Prognostic Biomarker for Refractory Epilepsy Following Treatment of Infantile Epileptic Spasms Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Refractory epilepsy is common among children with a history of infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS), yet no validated prognostic biomarkers exist to guide early risk stratification. The Burden of Amplitudes and Epileptiform Discharges (BASED) score is an interictal EEG rating scale for children with IESS, with scores of 4 or 5 suggesting epileptic encephalopathy. The objective of this study was to determine whether a post-treatment BASED score of 4/5 is a prognostic biomarker for refractory epilepsy after IESS treatment. This retrospective validation study of children with IESS was conducted at a Level 4 pediatric epilepsy center. Children with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) were excluded. Three blinded reviewers assigned 2021 BASED scores to full-length post-treatment EEGs. Refractory epilepsy was defined as persistent seizures despite treatment with at least 2 antiseizure medications or completion of epilepsy surgery. Prespecified performance benchmarks for BASED 4/5 as a rule-in test required ≥80% specificity and a positive likelihood ratio of ≥4. The cohort included 123 children (42.3% female), with a median first treatment age of 8.0 months (IQR 5.9-10.3) and follow-up duration after first treatment of 58.8 months (IQR 42.2-80.7). Only 11.4% had a favorable etiology. EEGs (median 19 hours) were completed at a median of 47 days (32-72) after starting treatment. The inter-rater agreement for epileptic encephalopathy was excellent (κfree = 0.78). Half (52%) of the children had refractory epilepsy. BASED 4/5 demonstrated high specificity (88.1%, 95% CI 77.1-95.1) for refractory epilepsy, with a positive likelihood ratio of 4.4 (2.1-9.1). The sensitivity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were 51.6% (38.7-64.3), 82.5% (69.3-90.8), and 62.7% (56.1-68.7), respectively. An exploratory composite indicator comprising BASED 4/5, persistent epileptic spasms, and/or epileptic spasms relapse demonstrated higher sensitivity (79.7%, 67.8-88.7) with modestly reduced specificity (81.4%, 69.1-90.3). Study limitations include the single-center design, exclusion of children with TSC, variable EEG timing, and shorter follow-up in some children. Nevertheless, in this independent validation cohort, a post-treatment BASED 4/5 demonstrated favorable prognostic performance consistent with its proposed use as a rule-in test for refractory epilepsy. These findings support a post-treatment BASED score of 4/5 as a prognostic biomarker for refractory epilepsy after IESS treatment.

papers.title: An Integrated Approach for Early In Vitro Sedation Prediction Utilizing hiPSC Neurons and Human Ion Channel Assays.
papers.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) liabilities remain a significant cause of failure in drug development. Two complementary in vitro safety assays were previously developed, combining automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and multielectrode array techniques, to detect and avoid seizurogenic compounds. Further to seizure risk, sedation and fatigue are commonly encountered CNS side effects during drug safety testing. Here, the aim was to extend the capability of the in vitro safety assay to enable earlier detection of sedative potential. Fourteen compounds with reported sedative activity and five non-sedative controls were screened in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons using multielectrode array. These compounds were further screened with automated patch-clamp electrophysiology using cells expressing CNS ion channels implicated in sedation: KV1.1, KV2.1, KV3.1, KV7.2/7.3, NaV1.2, K2P2.1, or the α1β2γ2 GABAA, and α4β2 nicotinic receptors. Known sedative compounds reduced neural firing and network burst activity in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-neurons, indicating sedative effects, whilst negative control compounds did not significantly change multielectrode array parameters. Of the 19 compounds screened, 94% were accurately classified. Automated patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed that several sedative compounds interacted with CNS ion channels within a 30-fold margin to their total therapeutic blood plasma concentration. These results support the use of the combined in vitro safety models for detecting sedative as well as seizurogenic effects, offering valuable human-based tools for early hazard identification and prioritization of drug candidates. These platforms are also useful for interpretation of CNS-related findings in vivo supporting the principles of 3Rs to minimize and replace the use of animals in scientific testing.

papers.title: Bridging the Gender Gap in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Machine Learning Approach to Screening Women for Moderate-to-Severe Disease.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) can lead to severe complications if left untreated. Several challenges hinder OSA identification in females, resulting in underdiagnosis and undertreatment in this population. This study aimed to develop a machine learning (ML) approach specifically tailored to screen women for moderate-to-severe OSA. A retrospective study was conducted using clinical records of 1,210 women who underwent polysomnography at our institution. Collected data included demographics, body metrics, nocturnal oxygen saturation levels, medical conditions, medications, laboratory measurements, and polysomnography results. Four ML algorithms were employed to classify participants into moderate-to-severe and none-to-mild OSA groups. Due to the high missingness of laboratory values in the whole cohort, two sets of models were developed: one utilizing all subjects but excluding lab tests, and another restricted to a subgroup of 383 participants that additionally incorporated hemoglobin and lipid profile alongside the other features. Without laboratory measurements, the best-performing model was adaptive boosting, which achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and accuracy of 0.811 and 76.03%, respectively. When lab tests were included, gradient boosting machine outperformed its competitors, with the above metrics reaching 0.872 and 84.42%, respectively. The promising performance of our approach underlines the potential of artificial intelligence in refining screening strategies for OSA in women. Nadir oxygen saturation during sleep emerged as a particularly strong predictor, reinforcing the central role of nocturnal hypoxemia in OSA risk stratification. Future research should focus on incorporating broader clinical inputs and using larger, diverse datasets to develop a highly accurate, robust model that meets clinical standards and is suitable for real-world implementation.
