papers.title: Diurnal cortisol, perceived sleep quality, actigraphic sleep and depression: an exploratory pilot in patients with head and neck cancer.
papers.abstract: In patients with head and neck cancer (HNC), perceived sleep quality, actigraphy-derived sleep parameters, depressive symptoms, and diurnal cortisol may represent related behavioral and biological processes. This exploratory study tested a priori associations among these constructs. Forty patients with HNC completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), wore wrist actigraphs, and collected salivary cortisol at waking and bedtime across a 6-day period. Separate linear regressions tested associations of PSQI scores with actigraphic sleep measures with depressive symptoms, and with cortisol slope, waking, evening and mean indices. Post hoc PSQI item analyses used Spearman correlations. Global PSQI scores were not significantly correlated with actigraphic sleep parameters. Poorer perceived sleep quality was associated with higher depression scores (r = 0.64), flatter diurnal cortisol slopes (r = 0.48), and higher evening cortisol (r = 0.40). Actigraphic sleep parameters were not significantly associated with depressive symptoms or cortisol indices, and depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with cortisol indices. Post hoc item-level analyses showed that poorer overall sleep quality and greater difficulty maintaining enthusiasm were associated with greater depressive symptoms, flatter cortisol slopes, and lower waking cortisol. In this exploratory pilot of patients with HNC, poorer sleep quality was associated with greater depressive symptoms, flatter diurnal cortisol slopes, and higher evening cortisol, whereas actigraphic sleep parameters were not. Global PSQI scores may help identify patients warranting further assessment for depression and treatment-related symptoms.

papers.title: Low-dimensional burnout risk classification in engineering students: the role of demand-recovery interaction features.
papers.abstract: Student burnout is a rapidly growing concern, with prior research linking its development to a wide range of psychological, behavioral, and contextual factors. Machine learning approaches have recently shown strong predictive performance for identifying burnout, but typically rely on high-dimensional datasets impractical for real-world use. Whether burnout can be reliably identified from a minimal set of variables remains underexplored. This study addresses that gap using a low-dimensional predictive framework in undergraduate engineering students. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, three classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) were evaluated across three feature configurations (Raw: all nine unengineered base predictors, including academic, demographic, sleep, and physical activity variables; Engineered: four demand-recovery interaction features; Full: Raw combined with Engineered) to test whether burnout reflects academic load alone or an imbalance between demand and recovery capacity. The Full configuration performed best: Logistic Regression and Random Forest exceeded a matched permutation-based null (Global MCC = 0.173 and 0.190, respectively, p < 0.05), while Gradient Boosting did not reach significance (MCC = 0.126, p = 0.066). Across 50 alternative fold splits, however, mean Global MCC for the Full configuration was lower for each classifier (Logistic Regression 0.09, Random Forest 0.16, Gradient Boosting 0.11), indicating that the primary-split estimates are upper-range. In addition, adding engineered features to Raw predictors did not produce a statistically distinguishable improvement in Global MCC for any classifier. Moderate Risk classification remained difficult across all classifiers and configurations, with most confidence intervals crossing zero. Permutation importance identified Workload-Sleep Strain as the most influential predictor in the Random Forest model, suggesting the engineered features capture meaningful behavioral patterns. However, because these variables are deterministic transformations of the raw predictors, their incremental contribution could not be confirmed statistically. These results offer preliminary evidence that a small set of sleep, activity, workload, and engineered variables carries predictive signal for burnout risk above chance.

papers.title: Evidence for decoder-label-regime-dependent effects of complementary leaky integrate-and-fire temporal-state decoding in motor-imagery EEG.
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery electroencephalography often provides limited subject-specific supervision. This study tested whether complementary leaky integrate-and-fire (CLIF)-family temporal-state decoding shows a decoder-level advantage after the EEG representation is fixed, how that advantage changes with decoder-label availability, and whether hard binary spikes are required. ANN-SEW, the artificial neural network comparator with spike-element-wise (SEW) residual topology, and SEW-CLIF received identical frozen attention-based temporal convolutional network (ATCNet) and filter-bank convolutional network (FBCNet) representations. The evidence chain combined BCI Competition IV Dataset 2a (BCI2a) development, retrospective OpenBMI replication, an internally pre-access-held-out BCI Competition IV Dataset 2b (BCI2b) evaluation, cross-entropy-only label-budget analyses, and a separate internally pre-access-locked BNCI2015-001 Session-A-to-Session-B evaluation. Additional robustness analyses included shared whole-sequence readout for parameter-matched gated recurrent unit (GRU) and temporal convolutional network (TCN) decoders, exact-gradient sigmoid-gated Soft-CLIF, equal optimizer-update budgets, a within-BCI2a binary sensitivity analysis, and computational profiling. Under cross-entropy-only training, SEW-CLIF exceeded ANN-SEW by 10.082 percentage points (pp) on BCI2a and 5.470 pp. on OpenBMI, while full-budget BCI2b remained near parity (+0.181 pp). The ANN-relative gap decreased as decoder labels increased and persisted under equal-update training. At 25 labels/class, exact-gradient Soft-CLIF exceeded ANN-SEW by 11.085, 8.479, and 5.809 pp. on BCI2a, BCI2b, and OpenBMI, respectively. With matched whole-sequence readout, hard SEW-CLIF was broadly comparable to GRU-Stat and TCN-Stat on BCI2a and BCI2b and modestly higher on OpenBMI. The internally pre-access-locked BNCI2015-001 evaluation showed the same attenuation, with a slope of -2.319 pp. per label doubling (95% CI, -4.118 to -0.604). CLIF-family temporal-state dynamics show a reproducible decoder-label-regime effect under frozen supervised representations. Hard forward discretization is not required for the ANN-relative effect, and matched temporal readout substantially reduces differences between CLIF and other continuous temporal decoders.

papers.title: Longitudinal perspective on the buffering effect of Tai Chi intervention against accumulated perceived stress and its sleep-improving effects among late adolescence.
papers.abstract: First-year university students stand at the close of WHO-defined adolescence (10-19 years), in mid-transition: leaving family, entering a new institution, and assuming adult academic and social roles. Stress during adolescence can have consequences that persist into adulthood. Most mental disorders begin by the mid-twenties, while higher levels of adolescent stress predict greater risks of adult anxiety and depression, academic dropout, and lower workforce participation and productivity. The 16-form simplified Tai Chi routine is easy to learn, but direct evidence of its effect in late adolescents is limited. This randomized controlled trial examined its effect on perceived stress and sleep quality. A total of 176 first-year undergraduates, all aged 18 years at baseline, at a university in Hangzhou, China, were randomly allocated 1:1 to a Tai Chi group (n = 88) or a no-intervention control group (n = 88). The Tai Chi group practiced the 16-form simplified routine three times weekly for 12 weeks (90 min per session: 30 min of warm-up and 60 min of guided practice); controls maintained their usual lifestyle. Perceived stress (Perceived Stress Scale, PSS-14) and sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, PSQI) were assessed before and after the intervention. The primary outcomes (PSS-14 and PSQI global scores at week 12) were analyzed by baseline-adjusted analysis of covariance. The groups had similar baseline characteristics. All 176 participants completed the PSS-14 and 168 had complete PSQI data. Within groups, both measures improved under Tai Chi (PSS-14 -3.28; PSQI -1.00; both P < 0.01), whereas perceived stress rose in controls (+4.47, P < 0.001) and sleep quality was unchanged. After baseline adjustment, PSS-14 scores were lower in the Tai Chi group (adjusted mean difference -7.48, 95% CI -8.80 to -6.17; P < 0.001), as were PSQI global scores (-1.17, 95% CI -1.87 to -0.46; P = 0.001). Exploratory component analyses gave nominal P < 0.05 for four PSQI components, none of which remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Compared with no intervention, a 12-week 16-form Tai Chi program lowered perceived stress and improved sleep quality in late adolescents starting university, buffering the stress escalation of the academic semester, and merits multicenter testing against an active comparator.

papers.title: Association between sleep patterns and diagnosed chronic kidney disease: a cohort study in China.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a globally prevalent and progressive health condition, with increasing evidence indicating a significant association between sleep quality and renal health. This study aims to explore the relationship between sleep quality and the development of CKD and to assess how various sleep characteristics influence renal health. This prospective cohort study included participants aged 30-79 years from 10 districts within the China Kadoorie Biobank. Sleep quality was evaluated using a standardized questionnaire that covered seven parameters, including delayed/disrupted sleep, waking early, sleep medication, daytime sleepiness, naps, snoring, and total sleep duration. Different sleep patterns were identified by k-prototype clustering analysis. Survival analysis and relative weight analysis (RWA) were employed to investigate the associations between sleep disturbances and the incidence of diagnosed CKD. Cluster analysis revealed three distinct sleep patterns. Compared with the Cluster1 (optimal sleep), Cluster 2 (frequent napping/snoring) (HR = 1.103, 95% CI: 1.027-1.185, p = 0.007) and Cluster 3 (short and fragmented sleep) (HR = 1.210, 95% CI: 1.129-1.297, p < 0.001) patterns were associated with a significantly increased risk of diagnosed CKD. However, after propensity score matching (PSM), the association for Cluster 2 was attenuated and no longer statistically significant, whereas the association for Cluster 3 remained robust. Of the seven sleep parameters, the top three contributors to diagnosed CKD risk were in order of importance as follows: snoring (RW = 2.59E-04, RS-RW = 55.49%, p < 0.05), total sleep duration (RW = 1.09E-04, RS-RW = 23.32%, p < 0.05), and daytime naps (RW = 4.12E-05, RS-RW = 8.81%, p < 0.05). Unhealthy sleep patterns increased the risk of suffering from diagnosed CKD. Short and fragmented sleep showed the most robust association, whereas the association for frequent napping/snoring was attenuated after PSM. These findings highlight the importance of improving sleep quality and addressing sleep-related problems such as snoring may help reduce diagnosed CKD risk and promote overall kidney health.

papers.title: Screening-positive subclinical eating disorder symptoms and associated factors among high school students: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Subclinical eating disorder (SCED) symptoms are common among adolescents and may be associated with adverse psychological and behavioral outcomes. However, evidence on screening-positive SCED symptoms and associated factors among high school students remains limited. Identifying these factors may support early screening and prevention. In December 2023, a stratified random cluster sampling method was used to recruit students from 12 high schools in Yangzhou, Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using a self-developed general information questionnaire, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire 6.0 (EDE-Q 6.0), the Ma Body Figure Scale, the Children's Depression Inventory-Short Form (CDI-S), the Spence Children's Anxiety Scale-Short Version (SCAS-S), the National Mental Health Literacy Questionnaire, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. BMI was classified using the WHO 2007 age- and sex-specific BMI-for-age reference for participants younger than 19 years, with adult WHO BMI cut-offs used for participants aged 19 years or older. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) with school as the clustering variable were used to examine factors associated with screening-positive SCED symptoms. A total of 2,681 high school students were included in the analysis, of whom 645 (24.1%) screened positive for SCED symptoms. In the school-clustered GEE model, female sex (OR = 1.351, 95% CI: 1.109-1.645), overweight (OR = 3.418, 95% CI: 2.632-4.439), obesity (OR = 7.740, 95% CI: 5.939-10.089), positive body image misperception (OR = 4.280, 95% CI: 3.533-5.184), higher depressive symptom scores (OR per 1-SD increase = 1.454, 95% CI: 1.297-1.630), higher anxiety symptom scores (OR per 1-SD increase = 1.387, 95% CI: 1.269-1.516), and poor sleep quality (OR = 1.393, 95% CI: 1.121-1.733) were associated with higher odds of screening-positive SCED symptoms. Adequate mental health literacy was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.609, 95% CI: 0.506-0.734). Approximately one-quarter of the participating high school students screened positive for SCED symptoms. Screening-positive SCED symptoms were associated with weight status, body image misperception, depressive and anxiety symptom severity, sleep quality, and mental health literacy. These findings support multidimensional school-based screening and health education while recognizing that the EDE-Q threshold identifies a screening-defined condition rather than a clinical diagnosis.

papers.title: Health Burden of Night-Shift Work Among Polysomnography Technologists in India: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Polysomnography technologists perform overnight sleep studies requiring continuous patient monitoring, technical management of diagnostic equipment, and sustained attention. Although night-shift work has been associated with adverse health outcomes among healthcare workers, the occupational health burden among polysomnography technologists remains poorly characterized in India. This study evaluated sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, burnout-related symptoms, musculoskeletal symptoms, and selected cardiometabolic indicators and examined their associations with years of night-shift work experience. This cross-sectional observational study used an online structured questionnaire distributed through professional groups to polysomnography technologists working in private hospitals and sleep centers in South India. Participants were graduates with at least six months of night-shift experience. Of 196 responses, 16 were excluded for less than six months of night-shift experience and 30 for incomplete questionnaires, leaving 150 participants for analysis. The questionnaire included the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI), and musculoskeletal assessment. Height and weight were measured by participants. Blood pressure was manually assessed, while fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) were obtained from recent laboratory reports. Poor sleep quality was defined as PSQI >5 and excessive daytime sleepiness as ESS >10. The CBI was analyzed continuously and categorized operationally as 0-49, 50-74, and 75-100. Years of night-shift work experience were analyzed as a continuous exposure and categorized as ≤5 versus >5 years. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for age, sex, and BMI. Mean age was 29.97 ± 4.43 years, and BMI was 24.16 ± 3.19 kg/m². Mean PSQI, ESS, and CBI scores were 7.09 ± 2.95, 9.20 ± 3.39, and 45.99 ± 20.95, respectively. Poor sleep quality occurred in 97 (64.7%), excessive daytime sleepiness in 56 (37.3%), and musculoskeletal symptoms in 126 (84.0%). CBI scores were categorized as 0-49 in 86 (57.3%), 50-74 in 48 (32.0%), and 75-100 in 16 (10.7%). Hypertension-range blood pressure was identified in 21 (14.0%) and prediabetes in 11 (7.3%). Each additional year of night-shift work experience was associated with higher odds of poor sleep quality (adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 1.433, 95% CI: 1.118-1.835), excessive daytime sleepiness (aOR: 1.205, 95% CI: 1.001-1.450), CBI ≥50 (aOR: 1.810, 95% CI: 1.350-2.428), musculoskeletal symptoms (aOR: 1.372, 95% CI: 1.003-1.878), lower-back symptoms (aOR: 1.296, 95% CI: 1.051-1.598), neck symptoms (aOR: 1.272, 95% CI: 1.043-1.552), and hypertension-range blood pressure (aOR: 1.387, 95% CI: 1.052-1.829). No significant associations were observed with shoulder symptoms or prediabetes. Polysomnography technologists reported frequent poor sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, burnout-related symptoms, and musculoskeletal symptoms. More years of night-shift work experience were associated with several adverse health outcomes after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design and potential residual confounding. Prospective multicenter studies are warranted.

papers.title: Associations of insomnia symptoms and physical activity with life satisfaction and psychological well-being among secondary school students in Spain: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms and physical inactivity are common during adolescence and may be associated with poorer well-being. However, their independent associations with different well-being indicators remain insufficiently examined in Spanish secondary school students. To examine the independent associations of insomnia symptoms and physical activity with life satisfaction and psychological well-being among adolescents, after adjusting for sociodemographic factors. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 462 secondary school students from six schools in Zaragoza, Spain. Participants completed self-report measures of insomnia symptoms, physical activity, life satisfaction, psychological well-being, and subjective social status. Hierarchical multiple linear regression models with bootstrap confidence intervals were used to examine the contribution of insomnia symptoms and physical activity beyond age, gender, geographical area, and subjective social status. The mean Insomnia Severity Index score was 9.08 (SD = 4.58), and 59.1% of students presented subthreshold, moderate clinical, or severe clinical insomnia symptoms. The mean PAQ-A score was 2.67 (SD = 0.77), with 57.1% of students classified as physically inactive. Insomnia symptoms were negatively associated with both life satisfaction and psychological well-being, whereas physical activity was positively associated with both outcomes. The addition of insomnia symptoms and physical activity increased the explained variance in life satisfaction and psychological well-being beyond sociodemographic covariates. Insomnia symptoms showed larger standardised associations than physical activity in both models. Insomnia symptoms and physical activity were independently associated with well-being indicators among Spanish adolescents. School-based strategies addressing both sleep health and physical activity may contribute to adolescent well-being, although longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify the directionality of these relationships.

papers.title: The impact of nesting care on the growth and neurological development of premature infants in neonatal intensive care units.
papers.abstract: To examine the associations of nesting care with growth, nighttime sleep-wake measures, and early neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm infants admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). This single-center retrospective observational study compared two noncontemporaneous cohorts at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Linping District, Hangzhou. Fifty preterm infants receiving nesting care from March 2024 to March 2025 and 50 receiving traditional care from February 2023 to February 2024 were manually selected from the eligible population to achieve approximate baseline comparability. Growth was assessed at birth and 3 months corrected age, sleep-wake activity by actigraphy at baseline and day 7, and neurodevelopment using the Gesell Developmental Schedules at 40 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA) and 3 months corrected age. Longitudinal sleep and Gesell outcomes were analyzed using adjusted change-score regression models with HC3 robust standard errors and Holm correction. At 3 months corrected age, the nesting-care group had higher body weight (difference, 195.12 g; 95% CI, 26.00-364.24), greater body length (2.04 cm; 95% CI, 0.68-3.40), and greater head circumference (median difference, 1.00 cm). From baseline to day 7, improvement in total sleep duration was greater in the nesting-care group (adjusted difference in change, 1.09 h; 95% CI, 0.36-1.81; Holm-adjusted P = 0.010), while mean awakening duration decreased more (-0.57 h; 95% CI, -0.70 to -0.45; P < 0.001). For neurodevelopment, adjusted improvements from 40 weeks PMA to 3 months corrected age were greater for fine motor (4.40 points), adaptive (3.95), language (2.18), and personal-social domains (1.60), whereas gross motor change was not statistically significant after adjustment (P = 0.054). In this retrospective comparison of noncontemporaneous cohorts, nesting care was associated with more favorable growth, nighttime actigraphy-derived sleep-wake measures, and several early neurodevelopmental outcomes. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because residual confounding and calendar-period effects cannot be excluded.

papers.title: Mediators of the association between physical activity and depressive symptoms in youth: a systematic review and meta-analytic structural equation modelling.
papers.abstract: Physical activity is consistently associated with fewer depressive symptoms in young people, yet the mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This systematic review and meta-analytic structural equation modelling (MASEM) study aimed to identify potential mediators linking physical activity with depressive symptoms in youth and quantitatively synthesise repeatedly examined mediation pathways. Six electronic databases were searched for observational quantitative studies examining physical activity, potential mediators, and depressive symptoms in children, adolescents, and young adults within a prespecified eligibility range of 6-27 years. Potential mediators were synthesised narratively and categorised into conceptually related domains. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted within the mediation-focused quantitative subset, followed by two-stage random-effects MASEM for mediator constructs with sufficient independent studies and complete correlation data. Eighty-seven studies were included in the broader systematic review, of which 80 formally examined at least one mediator and 39 contributed to the quantitative evidence base. Within this mediation-focused quantitative subset, physical activity was, on average, inversely associated with depressive symptoms (r = -0.234, 95% CI -0.281 to -0.187), although heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 98.29%) and the 95% prediction interval included zero (-0.499 to 0.070). Narrative synthesis identified potential pathways involving psychological resources and self-related perceptions, social factors, behavioural and lifestyle factors, cognitive-emotional processes, maladaptive behavioural factors, and physical or neurobiological factors. Construct-specific MASEM supported statistical indirect associations through psychological resilience (ab = -0.108, 95% CI -0.172 to -0.061), self-esteem (ab = -0.134, 95% CI -0.239 to -0.062), and social support (ab = -0.127, 95% CI -0.220 to -0.059). Sleep quality showed a significant indirect association in an exploratory model based on three studies. Psychological resilience, self-esteem, and social support emerged as repeatedly examined candidate pathways linking physical activity with depressive symptoms. However, the predominantly cross-sectional and just-identified MASEM models cannot establish temporal ordering, and alternative-direction analyses indicated that at least the resilience correlation structure was also compatible with a reverse indirect pathway. The findings should therefore be interpreted as statistical indirect associations rather than established causal mechanisms. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/recorddashboard, identifier (CRD420261355504).

papers.title: Differential associations of contralesional and ipsilesional brain functional connectivity with lower-limb impairment after stroke.
papers.abstract: Stroke may induce distinct plastic structural changes within the ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres of the brain, leading to interhemispheric imbalances in cortical connectivity. Maximum joint range of motion (ROMmax) impairments may also occur in the paretic limb, contributing to increased interlimb asymmetry and impaired gait. This study examined the influence of ipsilesional and contralesional brain functional connectivity on hip flexion ROMmax interlimb asymmetry and walking performance in stroke survivors. Eighteen individuals with chronic stroke (57.5 ± 14.8 years; 26.7 ± 22.2 months post-stroke) were assessed for functional connectivity of the ipsilesional and contralesional general hemispheres and specific primary motor cortex (M1) areas of the brain with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). Participants were also assessed for hip flexion active ROMmax of the paretic and non-paretic limbs and 10-m walk test, and ROMmax interlimb asymmetry was further calculated. Relationships between changes in these variables were examined by Pearson product-moment (r) and regression analyses. Hip flexion ROMmax interlimb asymmetry was significantly associated with contralesional functional connectivity in both general (r = 0.53) and M1-specific (r = 0.48) regions of the brain (P < 0.05). Walking performance was only associated with contralesional M1 connectivity (r = 0.51; P < 0.05). Contralesional hemisphere connectivity explained 28% of the variance in ROMmax asymmetry, while contralesional M1 connectivity explained 26% of the variance in walking time. No significant relationships were found for brain connectivity within the ipsilesional hemisphere. Greater brain functional connectivity in contralesional cortical regions is associated with increased hip ROMmax asymmetry and impaired walking performance in stroke survivors, highlighting the role of contralesional networks in post-stroke motor impairment.

papers.title: Report-derived interictal epileptiform discharge burden is associated with 7-day antiseizure medication decisions after pediatric video electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: To determine whether a three-level interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) burden abstracted from qualitative wording in issued pediatric video electroencephalography (VEEG) reports, rather than directly measured spike frequency, was associated with antiseizure medication (ASM) decisions within 7 days. This single-center retrospective cohort included 216 VEEG report episodes from 181 children. Two reviewers independently classified each report as showing no, low, or moderate-to-high IED burden while unaware of the standardized 7-day outcome; disagreements were adjudicated. We separately analyzed a diagnostic/initiation cohort for new ASM initiation and an established-epilepsy cohort for exploratory treatment intensification. Associations were assessed using exact and trend tests and logistic regression with patient-clustered robust standard errors. Agreement was 211/216 (97.7%); linear-weighted Cohen κ was 0.975 (patient-clustered bootstrap 95% CI 0.947-0.995). The diagnostic/initiation cohort comprised 113 reports from 112 children, with 36 new ASM initiations. Initiation rates were 13.0%, 42.9%, and 70.0% for no, low, and moderate-to-high burden, respectively (trend p < 0.001). The adjusted odds ratio per higher burden grade was 2.89 (95% CI 1.58-5.30; p < 0.001). The established-epilepsy cohort comprised 103 reports from 76 children, with 13 intensification events. Moderate-to-high burden versus none/low yielded an odds ratio of 4.73 (95% CI 1.31-17.08; p = 0.018), but complementary analyses were not statistically significant. Report-derived IED burden showed a strong graded association with new ASM initiation within 7 days. The treatment-intensification finding was exploratory. These data describe prescribing context and do not establish causality, treatment benefit, or an IED-based treatment threshold.

papers.title: Multiple platform-induced sleep restriction disrupts time-of-day-dependent corticosterone and leukocyte profiles in C57BL/6 mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep restriction (SR) is recognized to alter neuroendocrine and immune parameters, yet whether these changes reflect overall alterations in signal magnitude or temporal shifts in systemic dynamics remains poorly defined. We evaluated the effects of subchronic sleep restriction on the 24-h diurnal profiles of serum corticosterone (CS), total white blood cell (WBC) counts, and granulocyte-enriched proportions in mice. Male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to subchronic sleep restriction using the multiple-platform procedure or maintained under control conditions. Serum CS, total circulating WBC counts defined by FSC/SSC gating, and granulocyte-enriched percentages were measured across distinct Zeitgeber times and analyzed using two-way ANOVA with Holm corrections for multiple testing. Daily mean corticosterone levels and total WBC counts did not differ significantly between groups. A significant treatment × time interaction occurred for serum CS (p < 0.001), but time-point differences lost significance after Holm correction (p ≥ 0.06). Total WBC counts showed a borderline interaction (p = 0.050) with no time-point differences post-correction ≥, and CS-WBC correlations were not significant (p > 0.05). Conversely, granulocyte-enriched percentages exhibited a significant interaction (p = 0.002) and retained significant group differences post-correction at ZT5 (36.07 ± 2.57% vs. 18.10 ± 5.59%, adjusted p = 0.005) and ZT11 (53.03 ± 0.21% vs. 84.86 ± 8.64, adjusted p = 0.006). The multiple-platform procedure is associated with time-specific differences in serum CS and granulocyte-enriched percentages without altering the diurnal mean CS or total WBC counts. Lacking direct mechanistic measurements, these data reflect potential temporal variations under sleep restriction paradigms rather than established corticosterone-mediated regulation, clock disruption, or altered tissue homing.
papers.journal: Neurobiology of sleep and circadian rhythms

papers.title: Immediate Return or Overnight Stay? Sleep Responses by Postmatch Travel Strategy and Match Participation in Professional Football.
papers.abstract: Late European away fixtures can disrupt sleep, but the influence of immediate return versus overnight stay, and whether responses differ by match participation, remains unclear. Postmatch travel strategy would influence sleep quality and duration across the prematch, match, and subsequent nights, with responses moderated by match participation. Observational repeated-measures field study. Level 3. A total of 19 outfield English Premier League players were monitored across 10 European away fixtures (5 immediate return and 5 overnight stay). Self-reported sleep quality (1 to 7) and sleep duration were recorded on the prematch, match, and subsequent nights. Fixed-effects models examined condition, time, and match participation, with standard errors clustered by player. Sleep quality was lower than prematch baseline on the match and subsequent nights (both β = -0.62 arbitrary units [AU]; P < 0.01; g = -0.63). After overnight stay, sleep quality improved from the match to the subsequent night in players who participated and those who did not (β = 0.69 and 0.63 AU; 95% CIs, 0.37-0.90 and 0.47-0.91; P < 0.01), whereas no change occurred after immediate return. Across participation groups, sleep duration was lower after overnight stay than immediate return on the match night (β = -1.94 hours; P < 0.01; g = -1.26) and subsequent night (β = -1.02 hours; P = 0.02; g = -0.67). However, after overnight stay, sleep duration increased between these nights by 1.45 hours in participants and 1.43 hours in nonparticipants (P < 0.01), with no significant change after immediate return. Participation moderated sleep duration on both postfixture nights (β = 1.27 and 1.64 hours; P ≤ 0.04; g = 0.82 and 1.07). Neither travel strategy was uniformly superior. Overnight stay was associated with poorer absolute sleep duration but a clearer next-night rebound in sleep quality and duration. Postmatch travel should be planned case by case, considering itinerary, next-day demands, and individual match exposure rather than applying a single team-wide policy.

papers.title: Quantifying Menstrual Rhythmicity and Physiological Coherence Using Continuous Wearable Data.
papers.abstract: Continuous wearable data reveal reproducible physiological oscillations across the menstrual cycle. Peripheral temperature offers a physiologically grounded, low-burden signal to align and summarize cycle dynamics at scale, enabling investigation of how reproductive rhythms relate to broader physiological systems. This study aims to introduce a temperature-based cycle coherence score and test whether stronger temperature rhythmicity maps onto known sources of menstrual-cycle variation and relates to cardiorespiratory physiology and sleep. We analyzed nightly wearable data from 150,333 menstrual cycles contributed by 14,536 individuals using Oura Ring. For each cycle, peripheral skin temperature, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, and sleep duration were modeled using first-harmonic sinusoidal fits scaled to cycle length. We derived a cycle coherence score summarizing the strength, regularity, and temporal organization of temperature-based menstrual rhythms. Mixed-effects models quantified cycle-periodic structure; cycle-level coordination with other signals was assessed via correlations in oscillation amplitude, phase, and fit quality; and participant-level associations between coherence and demographic, anthropometric, and cycle characteristics were evaluated using regression. Peripheral skin temperature exhibited the strongest menstrual-cycle rhythmicity (partial pseudo-R2 = .379, reflecting variance explained by the harmonic terms), forming the basis for a cycle coherence metric capturing substantial cycle-to-cycle variation in rhythm strength, regularity, and timing. Rhythmic variation in other signals was weaker but showed modest coordination with temperature coherence. Mean coherence declined with older age (regression coefficient: β = -0.038 for ≥46 years), higher body mass index (BMI; β = -0.004 per kg/m²), cycle irregularity (β = -0.050), and hormone use (β ≈ -0.082); higher coherence was associated with lower resting heart rate (β = -0.246), lower respiratory rate (β = -0.027), and longer sleep duration (β = 0.062). A temperature-anchored cycle coherence score reflects meaningful variation in menstrual rhythmic organization and demonstrates that stronger temperature rhythmicity coincides with more regulated cardiorespiratory physiology and sleep.

papers.title: Learning and memory profile in pediatric craniopharyngioma with and without associated sleep disturbance.
papers.abstract: Children and adolescents with craniopharyngioma are at increased risk for visual field cuts, endocrinopathies, associated sleep disturbances, and cognitive challenges. While general intellectual functioning tends to remain intact within this population, the sellar/suprasellar location of craniopharyngiomas can disrupt important neural pathways essential for learning and memory. This study examines rote verbal learning and memory profiles - including nuances in learning approaches and slopes - in a clinical sample of pediatric patients treated for craniopharyngioma. Furthermore, the role of sleep disturbance on these outcomes is also explored. Retrospective data were collected for 17 pediatric patients with craniopharyngioma and associated endocrinopathies who underwent neurosurgical resection and irradiation (for all but one). As hypothesized, specific deficits related to rote verbal learning and memory were noted for the sample despite average estimated intellectual and adaptive functioning, while more pronounced learning and memory deficits were observed in the subset with reported sleep disturbances. Learning slope stagnation and/or decline across trials was observed in 75% of the patients, while post-hoc analyses revealed heightened susceptibility to recency effects (with poorer recall from the middle of the list) and a non-statistically significant trend toward increased intrusion errors, despite preserved semantic clustering. Findings underscore the importance of targeted memory assessment and multidisciplinary sleep management in this population.
papers.journal: Child neuropsychology : a journal on normal and abnormal development in childhood and adolescence

papers.title: When impulsivity goes wrong: Circadian timing distinguishes which night shift workers succeed and fail.
papers.abstract: Night-shift workers are at increased risk for accidents and injuries, and extant research has focused predominantly on the effect of sleep loss on low-level cognition as a mechanism. Much less is known about the effects of underlying circadian phase on performance, especially as it relates to accident risk. We assessed whether phase angle between circadian timing (dim-light melatonin onset) and task time predicted impulsivity (i.e. action bias, performance, and strategy) in night shift workers. To do this, we used the Stop Light Task, which simulates the complex, and real-world process drivers go through at a stop light (i.e. whether to stop safely or risk going at a yellow light). Thirty night‑shift workers completed the Stop Light Task approximately 13 h after an 8-h in-lab sleep opportunity, and underwent 24 h of hourly saliva collection to assess dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO). Results showed more time between DLMO and task completion (i.e. greater phase angle) was associated with worse performance (i.e. more crashes) and worse overall strategy in the context of risk. Phase angle did not predict action bias (i.e. propensity to run the yellow light), but post-hoc analyses showed greater sleepiness predicted reduced action bias. These results are the first to show circadian processes directly affect impulsivity in night shift workers and determine when someone is likely to be successful or fail in risky situations.

papers.title: Exploratory Pilot Randomized Crossover Study of Transcutaneous Vagus Nerve Stimulation on Sleep Quality and Mood in Healthy Adults.
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tcVNS) has been reported to influence autonomic regulation and sleep in various clinical settings. However, evidence in healthy populations is limited. This study investigated the effects of tcVNS on subjective sleep quality, mood, and autonomic function in healthy adults. We conducted a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial in which 29 healthy participants underwent two four-week stimulation phases (Active and Sham). Active stimulation was delivered at subthreshold intensity, whereas Sham stimulation involved identical device use without electrical current. Outcomes included the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index-Korean version (PSQI-K), Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D), and daily heart rate variability (HRV) indices collected using a validated smartphone-based application. Linear mixed-effects models were used to analyze questionnaire scores. PSQI-K scores showed a statistically significant but modest reduction during Active stimulation compared with Baseline (P = 0.013) and Sham (corrected P < 0.001), although the mean change did not exceed the minimal clinically important difference. No significant changes were observed for BDI-II or HAM-D. HRV responses were heterogeneous across participants, with no significant group-level differences. No serious adverse events occurred, and mild transient ear discomfort or tingling was reported by 3 participants (10.3%) during Active stimulation. This exploratory pilot trial suggests that tcVNS was safe and well tolerated and may produce modest changes in subjective sleep quality in healthy adults. The absence of mood effects likely reflects low baseline symptom burden. These findings provide preliminary, hypothesis-generating evidence that stimulation parameters may warrant further investigation, and confirmation in adequately powered trials and clinical populations is required. Clinical Research Information Service Identifier: KCT0009790.

papers.title: Validity of Actigraphy and Sleep Diary Compared With Home Polysomnography in Patients With Sleep Apnea and Insomnia Symptoms.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the validity of actigraphy and sleep diaries against home polysomnography (PSG) and to determine whether their performance differs according to sleep apnea and insomnia. Participants underwent one-night home PSG with actigraphy and next-morning sleep diary completion. Parameters included total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency (SE), sleep latency (SL), and wake after sleep onset (WASO). The apnea subgroup was defined as apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) ≥15, and the insomnia symptoms subgroup as Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index >5 and AHI <15. Mean differences, correlations, correlation comparisons, and agreement with PSG were evaluated. A total of 63 adults (mean age 49.7±14.0 years; 27 male) were included. Overall, actigraphy overestimated TST and SE and underestimated SL, whereas sleep diaries overestimated SL. Both tools were significantly correlated with PSG across all parameters, with sleep diaries showing a stronger correlation with PSG for SL (r=0.817 vs. 0.438, p<0.001). In both the apnea and insomnia symptoms subgroups, actigraphy was significantly correlated with PSG only for TST (ρ=0.594 and 0.462). In contrast, sleep diaries were significantly correlated with PSG for all parameters in the insomnia symptoms subgroup (ρ=0.668-0.781), but only for WASO in the apnea subgroup (ρ=0.440). Both actigraphy and sleep diaries showed validity relative to PSG, but their clinical use should be tailored to the underlying sleep disorder. Sleep diaries may be particularly informative in insomnia, whereas actigraphy may be relatively more useful in sleep apnea.

papers.title: Depression, but Not Anxiety, Is Associated With Poorer Working Memory in Adolescent Psychiatric Patients.
papers.abstract: The present study aimed to examine the associations between depression/anxiety and cognitive functioning in adolescent psychiatric patients to understand the progress of symptoms and build effective intervention plans. Data from 82 adolescents who received psychiatric treatment and psychological assessment at a university hospital were analyzed based on Wechsler Intelligence Scale and the Depression (DEP) and Anxiety (ANX) scales of the Personality Assessment Inventory (PAI). The mean full-scale intelligent quotient was 88.55, which was lower than the normative mean. The mean PAI DEP score was 65.45, and the mean ANX score was 60.10. In the correlation analyses, only DEP and the Working Memory Index (WMI) showed a significant negative correlation(r=-0.24, p=0.005). In a multiple regression analysis in which the three DEP subscales (cognitive, affective, and physiological DEP [DEP-P]) were entered as independent variables and WMI as the dependent variable. Only DEP-P, which assesses symptoms such as sleep problems, reduced activity, and low energy, significantly predicted WMI (β=-0.37, t=-2.90, p=0.005). Adolescent psychiatric patients presenting with a wide range of clinical problems reported more depressive symptoms and showed lower intellectual functioning than normative samples. In addition, the unique association observed between physiological symptoms of depression and working memory is consistent with previous evidence linking these symptoms to circadian rhythm disruption, dysfunction of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex/frontoparietal network, and white matter deficits. These findings suggest that therapeutic interventions targeting physiological depressive symptoms may contribute to improving working memory and academic achievement in adolescents.

papers.title: Validation of the 14-Item Shortened Version of the Positive and Negative Sleep Appraisal Measure Among Shift-Working Nurses.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a common condition that significantly impacts physical and mental health. Dysfunctional sleep beliefs and cognitive hyperarousal are recognized as key mechanisms in its development and maintenance. The Positive and Negative Sleep Appraisal Measure (PANSAM) was developed to assess cognitive interpretations of changes in sleep quantity. A shortened version, PANSAM-14, was created using machine learning to enhance clinical usability. This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric characteristics and clinical applicability of PANSAM-14 among shift-working nurses, a high-risk group for insomnia. A total of 299 shift-working nurses from Asan Medical Center completed an online survey including PANSAM-14, Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and Glasgow Sleep Effort Scale (GSES). Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), item response theory, and Rasch analyses were conducted to assess the construct validity, measurement precision, and item functioning. Reliability and convergent validity were also examined. CFA confirmed the four-factor structure of PANSAM-14 with good model fit indices. Rasch and graded response model analyses supported the measurement precision for most subscales, though subscale 4 showed lower item differentiation and reliability. PANSAM-14 demonstrated high internal consistency and significant positive correlations with ISI, PHQ-9, and GSES. Subscale scores increased in accordance with insomnia severity, supporting the scale's sensitivity and clinical utility. PANSAM-14 demonstrated acceptable psychometric properties for assessing sleep-related cognitive patterns, particularly among shift-working nurses. Its brief structure and acceptable psychometric properties suggest potential utility for clinical and occupational interpretation.

papers.title: Long-Range Temporal Correlations in Brain-State Dynamics via a Multivariate One-Hot Approach.
papers.abstract: Temporal sequences of discrete brain states provide a symbolic representation of large-scale neural dynamics. Here, we introduce a one-hot detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) formulation to quantify long-range temporal correlations in the recurrence dynamics of individual states, independent of the embedding geometry or the symbolic transition encoding. Applied to resting-state Electroencephalographic microstate sequences acquired under eyes-open (EO) and eyes-closed (EC) conditions, the method reveals heterogeneous scaling exponents across states and a global increase in scaling under EC, indicating condition-dependent modulation of multi-timescale organization. Systematic surrogate manipulations disentangle the structural sources of scaling. Disrupting state lifetime statistics through microstate duration equalization or randomization markedly reduces the Hurst exponent, whereas transition-order shuffling alone produces comparatively minor changes in absolute scaling. These findings indicate that long-range dependence is primarily associated with structured state lifetimes rather than with higher-order symbolic syntax. At the same time, transition ordering modulates EO-EC differences, suggesting that symbolic organization contributes to the context-dependent expression of temporal memory. Combined surrogate operations reveal additive effects. The proposed one-hot formulation provides a minimal, representation-invariant characterization of temporal correlations in symbolic sequences and can be generalized to discrete brain-state dynamics obtained from different neuroimaging modalities.

papers.title: Behavioral Manifestations and Diagnostic Challenges of Restless Legs Syndrome in Infants and Toddlers.
papers.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a sensory-motor neurological disorder, increasingly recognized in children, yet diagnosis in infants and toddlers remains challenging due to the reliance on verbal symptom reporting. This scoping review aims to synthesize the limited literature on probable RLS in infants and toddlers. A structured literature search was conducted using PubMed and Embase from inception through March 2026. Original studies, case reports, case series, and pediatric cohorts reporting probable RLS with onset or evaluation at ≤3 years were included. Reviews, editorials, and studies focusing exclusively on older populations were excluded. Thirteen studies were identified, of which 7 met inclusion criteria. Of the 7 publications, some focused on infants or toddlers, whereas others provided extractable data for children aged ≤3 years. Across studies, symptom onset was reported as early as 7.5 months in 1 cohort. Probable RLS in infants and toddlers presents as a behavioral sleep disorder characterized by nocturnal motor restlessness, accompanied by sleep fragmentation and distress. A characteristic pattern of awakening after 1-3 hours of sleep with motor agitation was frequently described. Periodic limb movements and low ferritin levels provide supportive evidence. Iron supplementation has been associated with improvement in symptoms in select cohorts. Probable RLS can manifest as early as infancy, presenting as a behavioral phenotype. Increased awareness of early behavioral manifestations and consideration of iron status may facilitate earlier identification and management. Future studies are needed to develop diagnostic frameworks and to better define the natural history of early-onset probable RLS.

papers.title: The effect of climate on epigenetic changes in psychiatric disorders: an evolutionary perspective.
papers.abstract: There is increasing evidence that epigenetic mechanisms of gene expression are dysregulated in psychiatric disorders. Epigenetic mechanisms can be modified by environmental factors such as climate. Climate is also known to alter circadian rhythms. This review article examines the possible effects of climate on epigenetic mechanisms of gene expression in patients with common psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder, from an evolutionary perspective. Implications for the mitigation of climate-induced mental illness are explored.

papers.title: A Novel Heterozygous KCNH2 c.1288G > C (p.A430P) Variant Causes Type 2 Long QT Syndrome Through Loss of hERG Channel Function.
papers.abstract: A novel variant in the KCNH2 gene (human ether-a-go-go-related gene, hERG) has been identified and is associated with type 2 long QT syndrome (LQT2). Integrating genotype analysis into clinical evaluation facilitates more accurate diagnosis and targeted therapeutic strategies for this condition. Sanger sequencing was used to detect the KCNH2 variant in an LQT2 family. The variant was transiently expressed in HEK293 cells for functional characterization via patch-clamp electrophysiology, Western blot, and qRT-PCR. A novel heterozygous missense variant KCNH2 c.1288G > C (p.Ala430Pro) was identified. Unlike wild-type (WT) channels, the A430P variant generated no detectable hERG currents. Western blot showed comparable protein expression between WT and A430P, both migrating at approximately 127 kDa, which corresponds to the core-glycosylated form. qRT-PCR revealed significantly elevated A430P mRNA levels compared to WT (p = 0.0027). The complete loss of channel function in the A430P variant is not due to reduced protein expression. The discordance between elevated mRNA and unchanged protein levels suggests post-transcriptional or translational dysregulation, expanding our understanding of LQT2 molecular mechanisms.

papers.title: A Biophysical Perspective on Microwave-Induced Neurobiological Effects.
papers.abstract: Microwave radiation interacts with the nervous system through a cascade of electromagnetic, thermal, and mechanical perturbations that drive a broad range of neurobiological responses. Although exposure guidelines are based on specific absorption rate (SAR), substantive evidence indicates that neurobiological effects arise across frequencies, waveforms, and SAR levels that SAR alone cannot characterize. We distinguish net-thermal, transient-thermal, and non-thermal mechanisms according to whether a response is mediated by the net temperature rise, by the heating rate and temperature gradients, or largerly independent of temperature change. This review traces the physical perturbation cascade from electromagnetic field distribution through thermal dynamics to thermoelastic stress, and reviews five biological endpoints: genotoxicity, molecular dysregulation and signaling, blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability, electrophysiology, and behavioral changes. A consistent finding is that many studies report associations with only SAR and frequency, omitting the intermediate physical quantities that drive the responses, and thus obscuring a mechanistic understanding of the causal chain. Mapping of reported studies into the SAR-frequency space reveals a clustering within the 0.9-3 GHz band and near SAR = 2 W/kg, with biological alterations reported below these limits under both continuous and pulsed exposures. These findings motivate future work that directly quantifies spatiotemporal physical perturbations to close the gap between exposure conditions and neurobiological outcomes.

papers.title: Bad Dreams and Eating Disorder-Related Impairment Among University Students.
papers.abstract: Sleep problems are elevated among people with eating disorder (ED) symptoms; however, there is little contemporary research on bad dreams and nightmares in this population. Students completed measures assessing ED-related impairment, sleep, depression, and anxiety. Ordinal logistic regressions were used to examine associations between ED-related impairment and bad dream frequency categories (i.e. past-month average of zero, <1/week, or ≥1/week). Greater eating disorder-related impairment was significantly associated with greater odds of having more frequent bad dreams, B = 0.61, SE = 0.08, OR = 1.84, 95% CI [1.59, 2.14], p < .001, after adjusting for gender and minoritized race/ethnicity. However, associations were smaller but still statistically significant after adjusting for depressive and anxiety symptoms, B = 0.23, SE = 0.10, OR = 1.26, 95% CI [1.04, 1.53], p = .02. Overall, findings suggest that greater ED-related impairment is associated with greater odds of having more frequent bad dreams. High frequency of bad dreams among those with ED-related impairment may be partially driven by comorbidity with other mental health conditions or general distress.

papers.title: SIRT7 Aggravates Chronic Sleep Deprivation-Induced Cognitive Impairment and Neuronal Apoptosis via Decreasing Succinylation and Cascaded Ubiquitylation of NFL.
papers.abstract: Insomnia affected one-third of the global population, but its molecular mechanism was not clarified. A chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) model was constructed in SD rats using multiple platforms over water. Hippocampal tissues were collected for ubiquitinomics and succinylomics. Sirtuin 7 (SIRT7) inhibitor was administered to elevate succinylation levels. Molecular experiments demonstrated the cascade reaction of succinylation and ubiquitylation, and Neurofilament Light (NFL)-binding ubiquitinating enzyme. Chronic sleep deprivation caused cognitive disorder of rats. Mostly, succinylation and ubiquitylation displayed a downregulated trend in the CSD group, especially double modification of NFL at K370 (succinylation site) and K267/281 (ubiquitylation site), whose protein level was upregulated in CSD rats. NFL was proved to be a target of SIRT7, a well-known desuccinylase. SIRT7 inhibitor weakened cognitive deficit, blocked neuronal apoptosis, decreased NFL expression, and increased succinylation and ubiquitylation levels, which were inverse in the CSD model and cells infected with SIRT7 overexpression adenovirus. SIRT7 suppressed not only succinylation but also ubiquitylation through K370 of NFL. Knockdown of NFL receded cognitive disorder and neuronal apoptosis. BRCA1 Associated Deubiquitinase 1 (BAP1) inhibited NFL ubiquitylation and subsequently degradation. SIRT7 inhibitor promoted succinylation and cascaded ubiquitylation, as well as disrupting the interaction between BAP1 and NFL, finally suppressing CSD.

papers.title: Dexmedetomidine Versus Propofol Induction for Sedated Radiologic Procedures in Patients With Trisomy 21.
papers.abstract: Patients with Trisomy 21 (T21) are more susceptible to sedation-related adverse events (AEs). Few studies address the risk of propofol or compare natural airway sedation regimens in this population. Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is less likely than propofol to result in AEs as it promotes a more natural sleep and less airway muscle relaxation. This study is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data. We queried the Pediatric Sedation Research Consortium (PSRC) Database from the years 2020 to 2025. The demographic characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. The incidence of sedation-related AEs and sedation failures were described by induction drug (DEX vs. propofol). Any medication used other than DEX or propofol were excluded. We performed a propensity score analysis comparing the DEX cohort to the propofol cohort. All the statistical work was performed using SAS 9.4. A total of 337 patients met inclusion criteria. The average age was 7 years. Forty-four percent of AEs were partial airway obstruction. For the bivariate analyses, the AE outcome variable is statistically significant with the medication variable (χ2df=1=33.249, P<0.001). Induction with propofol had a 5 times higher odds of an AE (OR=5.069, 95% CI: 2.829-9.082). After propensity score matching, there are a total of 216 matched observations. In patients with T21 undergoing radiologic procedures, the odds of having any AE are higher with induction using propofol compared with DEX. Greater consideration should be given for use of DEX induction for patients with T21 undergoing sedated radiologic procedures.

papers.title: The Impact of Psychological Therapies on Well-Being and Quality of Life in Adult Chronic Migraine Patients: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Chronic migraine is defined as ≥ 15 headache days per month, with at least 8 days meeting the migraine criteria. It profoundly impairs quality of life and is often accompanied by comorbid insomnia and emotional distress. Despite growing interest in psychological and behavioral interventions in chronic pain, these approaches remain understudied in chronic migraine. To systematically review the impact of psychological and behavioral interventions on quality of life and well-being in adults with chronic migraine, and to compare intervention types across a range of clinical, psychological, and functional outcomes. A systematic search of electronic databases was conducted to identify studies evaluating psychological interventions for adults with chronic migraine. Titles and abstracts were screened, followed by full-text review against predefined eligibility criteria. Due to heterogeneity in interventions and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was undertaken. Four studies were included, examining mindfulness-based interventions and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTi) across outcomes for migraine disability, well-being, and frequency. Mindfulness-based approaches demonstrated significant reductions in headache frequency and disability, along with improved pain acceptance and mood. Intervention therapy showed rapid and marked benefits; mindfulness following medication withdrawal saw improvements in psychological well-being and migraine frequency up to 12 months post intervention; combining mindfulness with transcranial direct current simulation (tDCS) suggested additive benefits. CBTi showed significant improvements in sleep quality, with delayed but meaningful reductions in headache days. Emotional outcomes such as depressive symptoms improved modestly; anxiety was less consistently affected. Empirical research evaluating psychological therapies for chronic migraine with well-being and quality of life outcomes is notably limited. However, existing evidence shows promising benefits for adults with chronic migraine, improving aspects of physical, emotional, and functional well-being. Mindfulness appears particularly effective in reducing migraine burden, while CBTi addresses sleep-related pathways. These findings support integrating these modalities into holistic, patient-centered migraine care. A stepping stone into the future of migraine management which highlights the potential of psychological therapy successfully improving well-being and quality of life in migraine management.

papers.title: Morphological and Mechanical Properties of Masticatory Muscles in Individuals With Bruxism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Bruxism induces repetitive loading of the masticatory muscles, potentially causing structural and mechanical adaptations such as increased muscle thickness, stiffness and altered viscoelastic properties. However, findings across studies using ultrasonography, elastography and myotonometry remain inconsistent, and no comprehensive synthesis has integrated morphological and mechanical parameters across multiple muscles and modalities. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the morphological and mechanical properties of masticatory muscles between individuals with and without bruxism. Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420261433530), Web of Science, PubMed and Scopus were searched for studies comparing masticatory muscle morphology and mechanical properties between bruxism patients and healthy controls. Two reviewers independently screened studies and assessed quality (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale). Random-effects meta-analyses (MD/SMD, 95% CI) were performed per muscle. Of 9 included studies, masseter muscle stiffness was significantly higher in bruxism patients (SMD, 1.87; 95% CI, 0.53-3.22; p = 0.006), while masseter and temporalis anterior muscle thickness showed no significant differences (p > 0.05). Diagnostic criteria strongly influenced thickness findings, with self-reported bruxism showing increased thickness and polysomnography-confirmed bruxism showing decreased thickness. Masseter muscle stiffness, but not thickness, is significantly altered in bruxism, suggesting mechanical properties may be a more sensitive and consistent indicator than gross morphology. PROSPERO, CRD420261433530.
